newsitem.title: USA: Eli Lilly posts big quarterly loss, but stock gains.
newsitem.headline: Eli Lilly posts big quarterly loss, but stock gains.

text.p: Eli Lilly Co. on Wednesday reported a loss of $1.73 billion for the second quarter and said costs related to its acquisition of PCS Health Systems were to blame.
But the company's stock price rose sharply on news the Federal Drug Administration will speed up its review of Lilly's application for raloxifene, a new drug to prevent post-menopausal osteoporosis.
The Indianapolis-based drug giant posted a loss of $1.73 billion, or $3.14 a share for the quarter ended June 30, compared with a profit of $345.7 million, or 63 cents a share a year ago.
Lilly disclosed last month it would take a $2.4 billion write-off on PCS, conceding it had paid too much when it acquired the pharmaceutical benefits management company for $4.1 billion in 1994.

"Clearly, thus far in 1997 (PCS) is making more than they did in 1996, (it is) not in a loss position," Lilly chief financial officer Charles Golden said Wednesday. "It is improving, but we have a long way to go."

The company also cited second-quarter costs tied to a settlement of its litigation over retail pharmacy pricing. But the losses were partially offset by a one-time after-tax gain of $296 million from the sale of its stake in a Dow Elanco agricultural chemicals joint venture to Dow Chemical Co.
Excluding the charges, the company would have earned $417.2 million for the period, or 76 cents a share, matching analysts' estimates and up 21 percent from the second quarter of 1996.

While Lilly has yet to win regulatory approval for raloxifene, the FDA's decision to place the drug under a six-month, rather than the standard 12-month, review was cheered by investors on Wall Street.
Lilly climbed $2.31 a share to $116.94 on the New York Stock Exchange on Wednesday.
The company also said it hoped to meet Wall Street earnings expectations for the year despite the expense of preparing to market Evista, the brand name for raloxifene.
Lilly said worldwide pharmaceutical revenues grew 18 percent for the quarter, to $1.86 billion, aided by an 11 percent increase in its sales of the anti-depressant drug Prozac.
The growth from Prozac occurred mainly in the United States, where sales surged 24 percent in the second quarter, to $459 million, following unusually weak returns in last year's first quarter.
U.S. wholesalers had scaled back their purchasing of Prozac in the second quarter of 1996 after stocking up on it in the preceding quarter ahead of a price hike, Lilly said.
Overseas sales of Prozac fell 17 percent, to $138.6 million, because of competition from generic forms of the drug, the company said.
